flow.label: device
flow.desc: Observe behavior on real hardware or a controlled emulator

flow.label: trace
flow.desc: Capture calls, traffic, and native execution paths

flow.label: analysis
flow.desc: Reduce traces to a model of what the system does

flow.label: test
flow.desc: Turn the model into a reproducible check

flow.label: verification
flow.desc: Confirm the result at the layer that matters

focus.title: Mobile security & reverse engineering
focus.body: I investigate Android APK, DEX, JNI, and native execution through tracing, emulation, and network analysis. I compare evidence from devices, tools, and backend systems rather than treating a few matching signals as proof of full compatibility.

focus.title: Application security & backend
focus.body: I work with APIs, realtime connections, and access boundaries. I check not only whether authentication exists, but when it happens: before reading data, returning results, or allocating limited resources. Changes are paired with negative scenarios and regression tests.

focus.title: Distributed workers & reliability
focus.body: I investigate task queues, concurrent processing, worker shutdown, and recovery of unfinished work. My focus includes task ownership, error classification, and safe updates across multiple service instances.

focus.title: Infrastructure & observability
focus.body: I work with Linux infrastructure, containers, OpenWrt, and network diagnostics. I test hypotheses against configuration, logs, metrics, and independent requests, separating routing problems from TLS, application, and external-service failures.

cases.title: Android integrity research: devices, native code, and emulation
cases.summary: A research environment for comparing native execution on Android devices and in emulation, analyzing protocol behavior, and checking server-side verification boundaries.
cases.context: I investigate the interaction between Android applications, native components, and backend verification in integrity and attestation flows. A central challenge is establishing which observations belong to the same execution and where device behavior diverges from emulation.
cases.approach: Align application builds, versions, profiles, and inputs; analyze Java, JNI, and native transitions; examine traces and network artifacts; and test how results propagate through worker and backend contracts.
cases.focus: Reproducible experiments, isolated diagnostic modes, and a clear distinction between local output and the response from the intended server-side verifier.
cases.disclosureNote: Private laboratory research. Sensitive artifacts are not published. This page does not claim a Play Integrity bypass, an accepted official verdict, or complete equivalence between emulation and a physical device.
cases.diagramLabel: Simplified flow: device, then JNI / native, then emulation, then server verifier
cases.linkLabel: Read case study: Android integrity research: devices, native code, and emulation

cases.title: Securing realtime connections
cases.summary: Authentication design for a realtime channel, covering client/server coordination, negative scenarios, and protection of limited connection resources.
cases.context: Protecting ordinary HTTP requests is not enough for a realtime interface. The connection itself needs a verifiable relationship to the correct session and predictable access-denial behavior.
cases.approach: Align the client and server protocol, authenticate before registering a connection, keep sensitive values out of URLs, and test invalid or missing credentials alongside reconnect behavior.
cases.focus: Verify the access boundary independently of business logic. An authentication failure should not become an endless retry loop or consume another user's connection capacity.
cases.disclosureNote: An anonymized account of engineering work. Service addresses, identifiers, specific findings, and the system's operational state are not disclosed.
cases.diagramLabel: Simplified flow: client, then authenticate, then register connection, then session
cases.linkLabel: Read case study: Securing realtime connections

cases.title: Predictable shutdown for distributed workers
cases.summary: Work on graceful shutdown, draining active operations, and safely returning unfinished tasks when a worker stops.
cases.context: Process shutdown is a normal part of a system's lifecycle. If a worker keeps accepting tasks or cannot distinguish task ownership, an update can leave work stuck or handled incorrectly.
cases.approach: Stop accepting new work, allow active operations a bounded drain period, and conditionally update only tasks owned by that worker instance. Check repeated signals and transport failures separately.
cases.focus: Observable shutdown behavior, regression coverage, and consistency between source code and running instances, rather than a green build alone.
cases.disclosureNote: This case describes engineering principles. Infrastructure size, traffic figures, configuration, and current deployment status are not published.
cases.diagramLabel: Simplified flow: signal, then stop intake, then bounded drain, then return owned tasks
cases.linkLabel: Read case study: Predictable shutdown for distributed workers

cases.title: Mobile SDK and protocol research
cases.summary: Research into mobile SDK behavior across application versions, launch contexts, network exchanges, and integration contracts.
cases.context: Requests that look alike can behave differently when the SDK, application, platform, or installation context changes. A version listed in documentation is not a substitute for examining a specific build.
cases.approach: Analyze application packages and integration code, compare network exchanges and version behavior, establish input provenance, and distinguish static conclusions from runtime observations.
cases.focus: Do not generalize from one application or version without a new experiment. Structural protocol similarity is not proof of end-to-end compatibility with an external service.
cases.disclosureNote: Laboratory work in owned or explicitly authorized environments. Private traces and requests are not published, and access to third-party systems is not offered.

cases.title: Security of asynchronous push integrations
cases.summary: Analysis of boundaries between APIs, queues, workers, and external push providers: result access, transport errors, and consistent task state.
cases.context: Accepting an asynchronous task does not establish that it was executed or delivered. Results and status endpoints need access checks just as carefully as the original request.
cases.approach: Examine API and background-processing paths, result ownership, caching behavior, and transport errors. Separate internal task status from evidence supplied by the external provider.
cases.focus: Safe result handling and accurate interpretation of status, without delivery promises that the provider has not confirmed.
cases.disclosureNote: An anonymized overview of the work, not a public vulnerability disclosure or a claim that every historical finding has been remediated.
cases.diagramLabel: Simplified flow: API, then queue, then worker, then push provider
cases.linkLabel: Read case study: Security of asynchronous push integrations
cases.topicsText: APNs · VoIP · API security · Async backend

cases.title: Network diagnostics and observability
cases.summary: Layered network diagnostics across routing, DNS, TLS, HTTP, and application behavior, rather than conclusions drawn from one availability signal.
cases.context: A website error does not necessarily mean a route is broken. A successful health check does not establish that a particular user workflow works.
cases.approach: Inspect effective configuration, run control requests, examine logs and metrics, compare alternative hypotheses, and use reversible experiments without unnecessarily changing healthy components.
cases.focus: Causality, control scenarios, and the distinction between network reachability, a service response, and a functioning application workflow.
cases.disclosureNote: Internal routes, addresses, and access details are not published. This website does not provide proxy or VPN services.
cases.diagramLabel: Simplified flow: routing, then DNS, then TLS, then HTTP, then application
cases.linkLabel: Read case study: Network diagnostics and observability

cases.title: iOS platform and hardware-backed attestation research
cases.summary: Study of how iOS hardware-backed key attestation, app attestation, and device-boot behavior work, on owned or explicitly authorized hardware.
cases.context: This work examines iOS attestation-related APIs and platform behavior. The aim is to separate client assertions, hardware-backed operations, and server-side checks, without treating application-level observations as proof of secure hardware properties.
cases.approach: Read platform behavior and framework interfaces, observe the network exchanges that carry attestation material, and align observations across operating-system versions and launch contexts. Treat a documented behavior as a starting point, not a substitute for examining a specific build.
cases.focus: Describe the mechanism and its boundaries precisely. Distinguish what the secure enclave establishes from what the surrounding application claims, and mark clearly where a conclusion is an observation rather than a confirmed property.
cases.disclosureNote: Private laboratory research on owned or explicitly authorized hardware. Sensitive artifacts and device identifiers are not published. This work studies platform behavior; it does not claim an attestation bypass or an accepted server-side result.

steps.title: Start with context
steps.body: Establish what is actually running: version, configuration, inputs, and environment boundaries. Documentation helps locate the path, but does not replace observation.

steps.title: Form a testable hypothesis
steps.body: Define which result would support or disprove an explanation. Aim for a reproduction before changing code.

steps.title: Keep experiments focused
steps.body: Prefer narrow changes and controlled experiments over batches of edits that make the cause of a result difficult to identify.

steps.title: Verify at the relevant layer
steps.body: Unit tests, integration tests, devices, and external APIs answer different questions. Success at one layer does not replace checks at the others.

steps.title: Limit disclosure
steps.body: Share methods and conclusions, not private data. Work only on owned systems or with explicit authorization.

layers.title: Local tests
layers.shows: The implementation satisfied the assertions exercised by the selected tests.
layers.misses: Real devices, real networks, and server-side enforcement.

layers.title: Device behavior
layers.shows: What the client does in the tested device or emulator environment.
layers.misses: Whether the server accepts, rejects, or ignores what it receives.

layers.title: External server verification
layers.shows: The observed outcome of the tested server-side verification path.
layers.misses: Untested requests and internal causes; a response alone does not explain the mechanism.
